title: The Ones Who Stayed

beats.text: Imagine handing your savings to a man about to lose more than half of it.
Nineteen sixty-two. Los Angeles lawyer Charlie Munger starts an investment partnership.
Eight years, not one losing year.
Then nineteen seventy-three: down almost thirty-two percent.
Your dollar is now worth forty-seven cents.
Your buddy Hank cashes out. Told you so!
So who's the fool, Hank or Munger?
Fourteen years: almost twenty percent a year. The Dow, five.
A dollar becomes twelve and a half.
You see, it's like leaving a movie at the scary part.
You paid for the whole film and kept the worst twenty minutes.
Hank kept forty-seven cents. Those who stayed got the whole ride.
Later, Munger put it bluntly: if you can't stomach a fifty percent drop,
you deserve the mediocre result you're going to get.

facts.claim: Munger formed the investment partnership Wheeler, Munger & Co. in 1962 (with Jack Wheeler); he was then a Los Angeles lawyer (founded Munger, Tolles & Olson in 1962; practiced law in LA until 1965)
Yearly results 1962-69 all positive (30.1, 71.7, 49.7, 8.4, 12.4, 56.2, 40.4, 28.3): seven-plus years without a losing year
A dollar after 1973-74: 0.681 x 0.685 = about 47 cents (arithmetic from the verified yearly figures)
1962-75 (fourteen years) compounded 19.8% a year vs Dow 5.0%
2009 BBC interview: if you can't handle a 50% decline ... 'you deserve the mediocre result you're going to get'
Hank is a fictional everyman inside the 'Imagine' frame; the movie is an analogy

caption:
1962: a Los Angeles lawyer named Charlie Munger started an investment partnership. Eight straight winning years, then 1973 and 1974: down about 32% and 31%. A dollar became 47 cents.
1975: up 73%. Over fourteen years, 19.8% a year against the Dow's 5%. Only the partners who stayed got it.
